entries.detail: SUBJECT is 'the session', so per the task instructions I audited the written record: GOAL_LOOP_INTERSTICE_HANGS_AND_AKIN_SOCIAL_2026-08-19_NOTES.md and the full goal-loop file beside it are the only account of the session available; I did not observe the session directly and say so rather than guessing. Item 0.2 of the goal loop (GOAL_LOOP_INTERSTICE_HANGS_AND_AKIN_SOCIAL_2026-08-19.md line 143) names two acceptable resolutions for the Amazon reader credential: a live carried profile, OR "a secrets driver fetch of the Amazon credential succeeded and a fresh sign in produced a profile." The notes section "What blocks Phase 1, and it is not code" (lines 45-56) record that the session confirmed the reader lands on the Amazon sign-in page and both Chrome's cookie store and the reader's profile carry an expired session mark, then conclude "The remedy is the product's own sign-in window, which takes a password, an emailed code, or a passkey, and needs the account holder" -- without recording that the secrets-driver fetch named as an explicit acceptable path in item 0.2 was ever attempted. I ran `grep -n -i -E "secrets-driver|request_grant|get_secret|grant_status|authenticate_grant"` over both the notes file and the full goal-loop file and got zero matches in either, so there is no record in this session's account that mcp__secrets-driver__request_grant / get_secret was fired for the Amazon credential before the session declared the item blocked on the account holder. This may ultimately be a legitimate case the broker cannot proxy (Amazon's own interactive sign-in with password/emailed code/passkey matches the global CLAUDE.md exception for identity the agent cannot proxy), but SEC-001 requires firing the broker BEFORE concluding a credential need is unresolvable, and the written record shows the "needs the account holder" conclusion was reached with no documented broker attempt for this credential.
entries.rule_title: Use the secrets broker, never ask the user to paste a secret

A similar issue appears on line 658 where key.password is logged.

entries.detail: Rule applies_to is **/*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}, so of the five targets only /Users/scottlydon/Developer/interstice/lib is in scope (43 .js files); the akin-server-side Swift targets (AuthorVisibility, Handler.swift, Subscriptions, Matchmaking) are a different language/framework and are not applicable to this rule. Read /Users/scottlydon/Developer/interstice/lib/auth.js in full (lines 1-149) and /Users/scottlydon/Developer/interstice/lib/server.js lines 560-640. Ran `grep -rln "createServer\|app.listen" lib/` which found only server.js, daemon.js, and doctor.js; daemon.js just calls createServer from server.js (server.js:121), and doctor.js's createServer is net.createServer (a raw TCP port probe, not an HTTP route table), so server.js is the sole HTTP route surface. In server.js:585-592, every request is passed through a single gate, `checkRequest(req, {port, token, pathname})` from auth.js, BEFORE dispatch to the routes table or any handler; a refusal short-circuits with 401/403 and no handler runs (comment at server.js:585-587: 'One gate, before dispatch, rather than a check inside every handler... a handler added later cannot forget to call something it never had to call'). auth.js's checkRequest enforces Host check, Origin check, and a per-daemon random 32-byte token compared with crypto.timingSafeEqual (auth.js:64-69, 106-116), refusing any request without a valid `x-interstice-token` header. The only exemption is isTokenExempt (auth.js:120-123), limited to the four static page-load paths ('/', '/index.html', '/panel', '/debug', '/debug/') that only serve HTML (which is how the token is handed to the browser in the first place) and never read or mutate state. I checked focus/stars-routes.js as a sample handler; it exports a pure function with no server binding of its own, so it too runs only behind server.js's routes table and thus behind the central gate. No second, ungated HTTP surface was found in lib/. This matches the rule's requirement that reachable actions/handlers be authenticated before reading or mutating data.</detail>
entries.rule_title: Server actions are authenticated exactly like API routes

entries.detail: Ran `rg -n '^(var|let)\s'` and `rg -n 'static (var|let)|nonisolated'` over all files in AuthorVisibility/, Subscriptions/, Matchmaking/, Controllers/Handler.swift, and `rg -n '^(let|var)\s+\w+\s*='` over interstice/lib/*.js plus state/, focus/, actuators/, video/ subdirs. Findings: Swift side has three mutable module-scoped statics, all in Subscriptions/NotificationDispatcher.swift and NotificationFanOut.swift: `retryDelay` (a fixed retry interval, test-configurable but not assigned from any request), `pusherOverride` (test seam, nil in production, set only by test code, not per-request), and NotificationFanOut.swift:235 `deliveryHook` (same test-seam pattern). Read NotificationDispatcher.swift lines 1-60: `enqueue(_:on:)` takes `plan: FanOutPlan` and `request: Request` as parameters and passes them straight into a `Task`; it never assigns request-scoped data (plan, request) into any static/module var, matching the file's own doc comment reasoning about not holding request-scoped handles past the request. The only Swift classes are Fluent DB models (MatchmakingProfileModel, ProfileSelectionModel, both `final class ... Model`, backed by rows not shared instances) and FanOutQueue, which is a ticket-keyed task registry, not a single shared field overwritten per request. JS side: the only module-level mutable var in lib/ is config.js:68 `let cached = null`, holding the parsed on-disk config file (app-wide settings), read via `loadCached()`; it is not assigned from any HTTP request, header, cookie, or session value, so it isn't request-scoped data leaking across users (interstice is a single-user local daemon, and this cache holds config-file content, not per-request payloads). No module-level var/let anywhere in the target set is assigned from request/header/cookie/session/param values.
entries.rule_title: Request data never lives in shared module state
